audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-002: Does verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch use byte-exact comparison for commitment deduplication to prevent hash collision attacks?
audit_items.state_context: kzg.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch delegates to ckzg4844.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch (C library). The C library performs deduplicate_commitments via memcmp (byte-exact). SidecarInclusionProven (Merkle proof) binds KzgCommitments bytes to proposer-signed block body before KZG verification.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The Go layer constructs commitment arrays from sidecar.KzgCommitments bytes and passes them to the C library without deduplication. The C library's deduplicate_commitments function uses memcmp (byte-exact comparison) over 48 bytes. Commitment bytes in accepted sidecars are guaranteed canonical because SidecarInclusionProven verifies a Merkle proof pinning KzgCommitments to the proposer-signed block body.
state_anomalies_found: No deduplication in Go layer before C library call — by design, C library handles this
Byte-exact comparison could fail for non-canonical elliptic curve point encodings, but inclusion proof prevents injection of non-canonical bytes
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching in this code path. Commitment arrays are freshly constructed per verification call.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: kzgVerifierRoutine is a single goroutine draining kzgChan. No concurrent access to commitment arrays within one verification batch.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Attacker cannot inject non-canonical commitment bytes because SidecarInclusionProven enforces bytes.Equal comparison against block commitments. The deduplication algorithm in the C library correctly handles duplicate canonical bytes. No bypass of batch verification is possible through commitment byte manipulation.
attack_scenarios: Inject non-canonical commitment bytes to bypass deduplication — BLOCKED by inclusion proof
Replay same commitment with different byte values — BLOCKED by Merkle proof binding to block
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: None. The inclusion proof check is synchronous and happens before KZG verification.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Reachable from P2P gossip and RPC paths, but the attacker's control over commitment bytes is bounded by the cryptographic inclusion proof. Any deviation from canonical commitment bytes would fail the inclusion proof check before reaching KZG verification.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Attacker can send DataColumnSidecar with any KzgCommitments bytes, but they must match the proposer's signed block body commitments via valid Merkle proof.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant that deduplication is performed correctly holds. The C library's memcmp-based deduplication is correct for canonical G1 points (unique compressed representation). The inclusion proof guard is sufficient to ensure only canonical representations reach the deduplication step.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: SidecarInclusionProven (Merkle proof against proposer-signed block body) + C library memcmp deduplication
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient. The inclusion proof pins commitment bytes to the proposer's block. Canonical G1 points have unique compressed representations, so memcmp equivalence implies cryptographic equivalence.
edge_cases: Test paths or internal reconstruction paths that bypass SidecarInclusionProven could allow non-canonical bytes to reach deduplication
Future code changes that relax the inclusion proof requirement would expose the deduplication to non-canonical input

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: The deduplication is correctly implemented in the C library using byte-exact comparison. The inclusion proof guard ensures commitment bytes are canonical before reaching the deduplication step. No vulnerability exists in this code path.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: Document the invariant that SidecarInclusionProven must always precede VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs to maintain the canonical-bytes assumption. Add a comment noting that deduplication is handled by the C library.

audit_items.title: Supporting Check: Does verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch_impl (SG-015) enforce unique commitments in its input list?
audit_items.state_context: The C library's verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch_impl (eip7594.c) explicitly handles duplicates via deduplicate_commitments using memcmp. This is specified behavior per EIP-7594 reference implementation, not a bug.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The checklist item claims the Go layer violates a pre-condition requiring unique commitments. Analysis of the C library source shows that verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch explicitly handles duplicate commitments via an internal deduplicate_commitments step. No pre-condition requiring unique commitments exists for the C API; duplication is expected and handled.
state_anomalies_found: Go layer passes potentially duplicate commitments (same blob appearing in multiple column sidecars for different columns) — this is by design
C library allocates unique_commitments and commitment_indices arrays sized num_cells to handle all possible duplicates
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No relevant caching. Deduplication happens fresh in each verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch call.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: No concurrency issues within the verification algorithm itself.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: No pre-condition violation exists. The C library's API design explicitly accepts duplicate commitments. Passing duplicates does not cause incorrect behavior — deduplicate_commitments produces correct unique_commitments and commitment_indices arrays used correctly in the random linear combination.
attack_scenarios: Passing N copies of the same commitment — handled correctly by deduplicate_commitments, weight accumulation in commitment_weights sums correctly

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: The code path is reachable but the alleged pre-condition violation does not exist. The C library's specification and implementation both explicitly handle duplicates. There is no pre-condition being violated.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: No attack surface because no pre-condition is violated.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant of correct batch verification holds with duplicate commitments as input. The deduplicate_commitments algorithm correctly builds unique_commitments and commitment_indices, and the subsequent weight aggregation and linear combination correctly account for duplicate entries.
edge_cases: Pathological case: all num_cells commitments are identical — correct, produces 1 unique commitment with accumulated weight

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: No pre-condition violation. The EIP-7594 reference implementation (c-kzg-4844) explicitly handles duplicate commitments. The Go layer's behavior of not deduplicating before the C call is correct and matches the C API contract.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No fix needed. Consider adding documentation comment to VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs noting that commitment deduplication is handled by the underlying c-kzg library.

audit_items.title: Supporting Check: Can a malicious P2P peer craft commitment bytes that bypass deduplication and corrupt weight aggregation?
audit_items.state_context: Two attack vectors: (1) Non-canonical G1 point encoding — blocked by inclusion proof requiring exact byte match against proposer's block; (2) Off-curve commitment bytes — C library rejects with C_KZG_BADARGS error (returns error, not false positive).

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The concern is whether attacker-crafted commitment bytes can bypass deduplication through non-canonical representations and corrupt weight aggregation. The critical state transition is P2P input → inclusion proof check → KZG verification. The inclusion proof step binds the sidecar's KzgCommitments to the proposer-signed block body using bytes.Equal comparison, preventing byte-level manipulation.
state_anomalies_found: Commitments not canonicalized (e.g., point normalization) in Go layer before C library call
C library validates commitment bytes in bytes_to_kzg_commitment during compute_weighted_sum_of_commitments, which would reject invalid G1 points
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: Inclusion proof cache (dv.ic) caches validated inclusion proofs by key derived from SignedBlockHeader hash tree root and KzgCommitmentsInclusionProof. Cached results bypass re-verification for seen sidecars.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: No concurrency issues in the verification path itself.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Two attack vectors analyzed: (1) Non-canonical G1 point encoding to produce different byte representations of the same point — blocked by inclusion proof requiring exact byte match against proposer's block; (2) Malformed G1 bytes (not on curve) — would cause bytes_to_kzg_commitment to fail with C_KZG_BADARGS, returning error (not false positive). Neither attack vector can cause incorrect acceptance of invalid data.
attack_scenarios: Non-canonical commitment bytes: BLOCKED — inclusion proof requires bytes.Equal against block commitments
Off-curve commitment bytes: BLOCKED — C library rejects with C_KZG_BADARGS error (returns error, not false true)
Two sidecars for same block with different commitment bytes: IMPOSSIBLE — inclusion proof anchors bytes to block

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Input canonicalization attack is unreachable due to the inclusion proof pre-condition. The only path where non-canonical bytes could reach the deduplication step is through internal code paths (reconstruction, local generation) that bypass SidecarInclusionProven — these paths use trusted data, not attacker input.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Attacker-controlled commitment bytes must pass inclusion proof (Merkle proof against signed block) before reaching KZG verification.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant that only canonical commitment bytes reach the deduplication algorithm holds. The inclusion proof (SidecarInclusionProven) acts as a cryptographic commitment to the exact byte representation of KzgCommitments. The C library also validates G1 point encoding in bytes_to_kzg_commitment, providing defense in depth.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: SidecarInclusionProven + C library G1 point validation in bytes_to_kzg_commitment
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient for all attacker-controlled paths. Internal paths use trusted data.
edge_cases: If a proposer creates a block with malformed commitment bytes (compromised proposer), the sidecar would pass inclusion proof but fail C library G1 validation — correct rejection behavior

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: No exploitable canonicalization vulnerability. Inclusion proof prevents injection of non-canonical bytes from external attackers. C library's G1 point validation handles malformed bytes from any source. No false-positive acceptance is possible.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: Document the dependency: VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs must only be called after SidecarInclusionProven to maintain the canonical-bytes invariant. Consider adding an assertion or type-system enforcement.

audit_items.title: Supporting Check: What is the consensus impact if a validator node accepts a batch proof with incorrect deduplication?
audit_items.state_context: verifyKzgBatch merges ALL pending data columns from ALL submitters into one call. Single verification result propagated to ALL submitters. One invalid column from any peer causes batch failure for all. Fallback (validateUnbatchedColumnsKzg) re-verifies each submitter's columns individually — prevents false rejection but incurs O(batch_size) CPU overhead per poisoning event.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The batch KZG verifier (kzgVerifierRoutine) drains kzgChan and merges all pending submitters' data columns into one verification call. A single invalid column from any peer causes the entire batch to fail. While there is a fallback that re-verifies each submitter's columns individually, this re-verification is unbatched (less efficient) and processes each submitter independently. A malicious peer can force O(n) expensive individual re-verifications per batch window by submitting invalid data.
state_anomalies_found: Single shared result propagated to all batch submitters — DoS amplification potential
Fallback to unbatched verification when batch fails — CPU cost scales with number of honest concurrent submitters
No rate limiting or per-peer quota on kzgChan submissions visible in the code
Batch window is determined by channel drain rate (default case in inner select) — any pending message starts unbatched fallback
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: seenDataColumnCache is checked AFTER KZG verification in validateDataColumn. Cache does not prevent duplicate processing of KZG proofs for the same column before it is marked seen.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: Multiple goroutines call validateDataColumn concurrently (one per gossip message). All send to s.kzgChan. kzgVerifierRoutine processes them serially but batches concurrent arrivals. The concurrent arrival rate determines batch sizes.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Attack: Malicious peer P_attack submits invalid columns at high rate. Honest peers P_1...P_n submit valid columns concurrently. In each batch window, P_attack's invalid column is merged with P_1...P_n's valid columns. Batch fails. Fallback verifies each submitter's columns individually: P_1...P_n each get correct Accept, P_attack gets Reject. But the unbatched fallback costs n times more CPU than the batched path. Under sustained attack, validator's KZG verification thread is continuously running at full unbatched cost.
phase2_symbolic_execution.counterexample: Attacker submits 1 invalid DataColumnSidecar per batch window. With 64 honest peers submitting in the same window, each batch forces 65 individual VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs calls instead of 1 batched call. This is a 65x CPU amplification of KZG verification work from a single invalid column per window. At 12s slots with multiple batch windows per slot, sustained attack forces continuous unbatched verification across all validator node KZG operations.
attack_scenarios: Single malicious peer spoiling batches continuously, forcing unbatched fallback for all honest peers in same window
Multiple malicious peers saturating kzgChan to maximize batch contamination
Targeting the kzgVerifierRoutine batch window to maximize co-mingling with honest submissions
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: Attack effectiveness depends on timing: attacker must submit invalid columns that arrive in the same batch window as honest submitters. The kzgVerifierRoutine drains all pending messages before processing.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Fully reachable from P2P gossip. Any Ethereum node can submit DataColumnSidecars over gossipsub. The attacker only needs to be connected to the target validator node. The malicious column must pass ValidFields() (structural check) but need not have a valid KZG proof.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Any P2P peer can send DataColumnSidecars. Structural validity (index range, length checks) is trivially satisfiable. Invalid KZG proof is sufficient to trigger batch poisoning.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant that valid columns are not incorrectly rejected HOLDS due to the fallback mechanism. The invariant that verification is computationally bounded FAILS under adversarial conditions. The fallback provides correctness but not liveness under sustained attack.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: validateWithKzgBatchVerifier fallback: validateUnbatchedColumnsKzg called when batch verification fails
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient for CORRECTNESS (valid columns not wrongly rejected). INSUFFICIENT for DoS resistance. The fallback increases CPU cost by up to O(batch_size) per invalid column submission.
edge_cases: If kzgChan becomes full due to high submission rate, validateWithKzgBatchVerifier blocks and the slot-duration timeout causes ValidationIgnore — legitimate columns lost
Under extreme load, the fallback verification itself can timeout (SecondsPerSlot timeout), causing ValidationIgnore for legitimate columns

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: Exploitable DoS vector: malicious P2P peers can force CPU amplification on validator nodes by poisoning KZG verification batches. The batch merging of data from multiple untrusted peers without isolation allows one bad actor to degrade performance for all concurrent honest submitters. Under sustained attack, this can delay attestation processing and block validation, potentially affecting validator performance scores.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: 1) Isolate batch failures: track which submitter contributed which columns and only fall back for the submitter whose columns failed. 2) Add per-peer rate limiting on kzgChan submissions. 3) Consider verifying submitters' columns independently in separate batches rather than merging all pending columns.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.severity_estimate: Medium — DoS on validator KZG verification performance, not a correctness/consensus violation. Fallback correctly validates legitimate columns.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-002: Are all commitment_indices validated to be within bounds of the deduplicated commitments array before array access?
audit_items.state_context: Two distinct index types: (1) cell_indices (Go-level, column position [0,127]) passed by Go layer; (2) commitment_indices (C-level, unique commitment position [0,num_unique-1]) generated internally by C library's deduplicate_commitments. Attacker never controls commitment_indices directly. Both bounds are independently verified.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The checklist concern is about commitment_indices being out of bounds. Analysis reveals two distinct index types: (1) cell_indices passed by Go (sidecar.Index, column indices [0,127]), and (2) commitment_indices generated internally by the C library's deduplicate_commitments function (sequential IDs [0, num_unique-1]). The Go layer passes cell_indices; the C library generates commitment_indices. Attacker never controls commitment_indices directly.
state_anomalies_found: Terminology confusion between cell_indices (Go-level, column position) and commitment_indices (C-level, unique commitment position)
No explicit Go-level check that cell_indices are in bounds before C call, but VerifyDataColumnSidecar provides this check
commitment_indices are internally generated, always in-bounds by construction
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching relevant to bounds checking.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Attempted to construct an out-of-bounds access via: (1) crafting sidecar.Index >= 128 — BLOCKED by VerifyDataColumnSidecar (ErrIndexTooLarge) which is called before KZG verification; (2) providing cell_indices > CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB to C library — BLOCKED by both Go check and C library sanity check; (3) manipulating commitment_indices to be out-of-bounds — IMPOSSIBLE since these are generated internally as sequential indices. No out-of-bounds access is achievable.
attack_scenarios: sidecar.Index = 128 (out of bounds): BLOCKED by VerifyDataColumnSidecar before KZG path
cell_indices[i] = 128 reaching C library: BLOCKED by VerifyDataColumnSidecar (same check)
commitment_indices out of bounds: IMPOSSIBLE — internally generated as [0, num_unique-1] where num_unique <= num_cells

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Out-of-bounds access path is unreachable. Both the Go pre-check and the C library check enforce identical bounds [0, 127]. The internally generated commitment_indices cannot be attacker-influenced.
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: No attack surface for out-of-bounds access.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant that all array accesses are in-bounds holds with two independent guards. The Go-level VerifyDataColumnSidecar enforces cell_index < 128. The C-level sanity check enforces cell_indices[i] < CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB=128. The commitment_indices are generated as sequential counters [0, num_unique-1] and used to index commitment_weights where commitment_weights is sized >= num_unique — always in-bounds.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: VerifyDataColumnSidecar (Go, checked before KZG path) + C library sanity check (defense in depth)
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient. Both guards are effective. Defense in depth provides protection even if one guard is bypassed.
edge_cases: NumberOfColumns config mismatch with CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB: if params.BeaconConfig().NumberOfColumns were set to value > 128, Go allows cell_indices up to that value, but C library would reject anything >= 128 with C_KZG_BADARGS — still safe

NumberOfColumns set to 0: VerifyDataColumnSidecar would pass any index (0 >= 0 is false for uint), allowing unbounded indices — but C library catches this. Config validation at startup should prevent NumberOfColumns=0.

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: No out-of-bounds array access is possible. Cell indices are validated at the Go layer before reaching the C library. Commitment indices are internally generated and cannot be attacker-controlled. Both the Go and C layers enforce the same bounds independently.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: Consider adding a comment documenting the dual-layer bounds checking. For the edge case where NumberOfColumns=0 (invalid config), add a config validation check to ensure NumberOfColumns > 0 at startup.
